### What is the areas you would like to add the new feature to?

Notation CLI

### Is your feature request related to a problem?

Currently only a few registries support artifact manifests, but all the registries support image manifests. Notation CLI stores signatures using artifact manifest by default, so there is a portability issue when copying signatures from registries with artifact manifest support to registries do not support it. The experience is broken. Since rc.2, a flag named `--signature-manifest` was introduced for users to select the default manifest, but users need to know what manifest type that registries support. 

### What solution do you propose?

The proposal is for Notation CLI to store signatures using image manifest by default. The UX is improved since It works for most registries without additional configuration, and users don't need to learn what manifest type supported by the target registry.

### What alternatives have you considered?

No alternatives.

### Any additional context?

_No response_

### What is the areas you experience the issue in?

Notation CLI

### What is not working as expected?

Currently [Referrer API](https://github.com/opencontainers/distribution-spec/blob/v1.1.0-rc1/spec.md#listing-referrers) is by default verified by Notation since `v1.0.0-rc.4`. For example, when using `notation sign`, if registries support referrer API, notation will not use an image index pushed to a tag described by the [referrers tag schema](https://github.com/opencontainers/distribution-spec/blob/main/spec.md#referrers-tag-schema). Since OCI spec 1.1 (including both image spec and distribution spec) is not officially released yet, support of Referrer API could lead to breaking changes or portability issue after Notation v1 is released. On the other hand, users may be confused that sometimes image index is pushed, sometimes not, which is an issue of consistency.

### What did you expect to happen?

Mark feature "support OCI Referrer API" as experimental feature, and document it properly. Users can use experimental features only after env variable `NOTATION_EXPERIMENTAL=1` is set. _x000D_
The default behavior of Notation is always using an image index pushed to a tag described by the [referrers tag schema](https://github.com/opencontainers/distribution-spec/blob/v1.1.0-rc2/spec.md#referrers-tag-schema). If users set env variable `NOTATION_EXPERIMENTAL=1`, Notation will check the support of OCI referrer API first, if registries support Referrer API, then notation will not push image index; if registries don't support Referrer API, notation will push image index as the default behavior. _x000D_


### How can we reproduce it?

N/A

### Describe your environment

WSL

### What is the version of your Notation CLI or Notation Library?

Notation `v1.0.0-rc.4`

To me, `notation verify` should not attempt referrers API without `NOTATION_EXPERIMENTAL=1` since the referrers API itself is instable / experimental. Yeah, after discussion with Shiwei offline, I agree with the above design. The `automatic fallback from referrers API to tag schema` is a part of the Referrers API's [spec](https://github.com/opencontainers/distribution-spec/blob/main/spec.md#listing-referrers). As long as a user attempts the Referrers API, the process should include the fallback mechanism to align with the spec. From this point of view, I think we can still claim that Notation is deterministic regarding the use of Referrers API and Referrers tag schema. @priteshbandi What do you think?
FeynmanZhou: @shizhMSFT 's proposal makes sense to me. Using a new experimental flag `--allow-referrers-api` to all registry-related commands will provide a consistent experience for signing and verification. My only concern is that this is a breaking change for users still using v1.0.0-RC.4 with Referrers API by default. They have to add this additional experimental flag `--allow-referrers-api` when verifying their legacy signatures after upgrading to v1.0.0-RC.4. We may need to document the considerations in the v1.0.0-RC.5 release note and elaborate on related docs. @priteshbandi @Two-Hearts @yizha1 @sajayantony

If it return 2xx then sign using referrers.~ * If referrers API returns 2xx, sign using referrers * If referrers API returns 404, fallback or the OCI-Subject header was not set, fallback and use tag schema * If referrers API returns anything else, fail the operation * For verify/inspect/list list, etc use referrers API first to pull the signature. * If referrers API returns 2xx use it to list signatures * If referrers API returns 404 or the OCI-Subject header was not set, fallback and use tag schema to list signatures * If referrers API returns anything else, fail the operation ----- @FeynmanZhou Had similar discussion with @toddysm on Thursday, IMO we should mark RC4 as deprecated ASAP and ask customers to directly jump to rc5 from rc3. cc: @iamsamirzon

column28: In implementing a ledger for OIDC public key, we've found that according to spec, the `kid` is only mandatory if there is more than one key on the JWKS endpoint, and only needs to be unique for each HTTP response on that endpoint. `kid` is obviously super important when trying to lookup the public key given an OPK. I was wondering if adding a hash of the OP public key to the OPK header would solve this? Any other ideas?

I've gone back and forth several times. I am leaning toward always including the jkt as part of the OP unprotected header. My notes follow. ## Encodings and key name Before we look at where to put them. I want to examine some options for how to encode the hash of the OP public key: `JKT ( JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint) from [RFC-7638 JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7638.html) is standardizes how to hash and represent a JWK such as the ones used in OpenID Connect JWKS URIs. * While early versions of the drafts references a JOSE header field with the `jkt` this is not in the latest version of the standard and `jkt` is not registered at the IANA protocol registry for[ JOSE Headers (JSON Web Signature and Encryption Header Parameters) ](https://www.iana.org/assignments/jose/jose.xhtml#web-signature-encryption-header-parameters). * However `jkt` is registered in the IANA protocol registry for[ JWK (JSON Web Keys) under JWT Confirmation Methods](https://www.iana.org/assignments/jwt/jwt.xhtml#claims) as JWK SHA-256 Thumbprint. [RFC 9449 OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession (DPoP)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449.html#name-jwk-thumbprint-confirmation) shows `jkt` being used as a JWT claim. ```json { "sub":"someone@example.com", "iss":"https://server.example.com", "nbf":1562262611, "exp":1562266216, "cnf": { "jkt":"0ZcOCORZNYy-DWpqq30jZyJGHTN0d2HglBV3uiguA4I" } } ``` JWS does have a JOSE header field specifically for that purpose called: (X.509 Certificate SHA-256 Thumbprint). ["x5t#S256"](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7515#section-4.1.8) (X.509 Certificate SHA-256 Thumbprint)) > The "x5t#S256" (X.509 certificate SHA-256 thumbprint) Header Parameter is a base64url-encoded SHA-256 thumbprint (a.k.a. digest) of the DER encoding of the X.509 certificate [RFC5280] corresponding to the key used to digitally sign the JWS. Note that certificate thumbprints are also sometimes known as certificate fingerprints. Use of this Header Parameter is OPTIONAL. However OPs may not always provide X.509 DER encodings of their public keys and I am concerned with introducing the complexity of serializing a JWK at an JWKS URI to a X.509 DER encoding. It is unclear what the canonical form of JWK to X.509 serialization is since x509s have fields that don't depend on the JWKs. I would suggest using the `jkt` key and encoding the OPs public key according to RFC-7638 JSON Web Key (JWK) Thumbprint. ## Where to put the hash? The nicest solution would be to put the OP (OpenID Provider) public key in the CIC commitment in the nonce that the user's client sends to the OP. Unfortunately that won't work because the user's client doesn't know what public key the OP will use to sign their ID Token until the OP returns the ID Token to the user. Let's look consider the various options: ### Store JKT in unsigned header of the OP **Pros:** 1. It is simple, and it works 2. Since it is unsigned, it can be added at any point by any party and parties that don't care about `jtk` can discard it without breaking signature verification. 3. The use of jkt here very clearly refers to the OP's public key. **Cons:** 1. It introduces unsigned headers which have repeatedly been misused by implementers and resulted in a number of security vulnerabilities. 2. Someone could prove the OP signature is incorrect by adding an bad jtk to the unprotected header. This could cause problems for systems that verify a signature, certificate once and then cache that outcome as they would conclude the PK Token is invalid and then reject it when it shows up without the bad jtk. 3. Parties can discard it without breaking signature verification. Potentially breaking long term verification without realizing it. 4. It would be nice to only have protected headers in PK Tokens so we never have to think about unsigned fields. ### Store JKT as an extended claim in Protected header of the CIC After getting the ID Token, the user's client would add the jtk to the protected header of the CIC. **Pros:** 1. Covered by the CIC signature. 2. This can be a standard part of PK Token creation to address issues where an misconfigured OP reuses a kid. **Cons:** 1. It break the rule the CIC commitment in the nonce is always the same as the protected header of the CIC and thus is always committed to in the nonce. This is not a technical limitation, but just would be an exception to how we treat the values in the CIC. 2. It isn't clear that jkt refers to the OPs public key. One might assume that since it is in CIC protected header next to the user's public key, that it is the thumbprint of the user's public key. ### Store JKT an additional signature in the PK Token After getting the ID Token, the user would sign and add two signatures to the PK Token. The first signature would be the CIC. The second signature would be the CICA (CIC After) which includes claims made after the ID Token is issued. This could be refreshed ID Tokens, signed select disclosures or any other claims a user's client may wish to make after the original ID Token issuance. **Pros:** 1. Works and is fairly clear. **Cons:** 1. Adds another signature, increasing the size of the PK Token. 2. Parties can discard it without breaking signature verification. Potentially breaking long term verification without realizing it. 3. Feels inconsistent to have this extra signature which only shows up because the OP doesn't have a kid. | jonnystoten: I'm in favor of "Store JKT in unsigned header of the OP". I don't think the cons are very strong for that option.

column26: Design for Gitlab CI support
column28:
As discussed in [Issue 26: Add GitLab CI signing example](https://github.com/openpubkey/openpubkey/issues/26) the approach used to sign software artifacts in github can not be used with gitlab because the gitlab workload can not specify the aud (audience) claim. Instead an aud claim is hardcoded in the workload configuration YAML. In this issue we propose the following design for gitlab and other settings where there is no client specified nonce or audience field._x000D_
_x000D_
## Generating a PK Token in Gitlab_x000D_
_x000D_
To generate a PK Token:_x000D_
1. The workload creates a key pair, (upk, usk), and requests an ID Token from the OP (gitlab)._x000D_
2. On receiving the ID Token from gitlab, the workload: generates the CIC (upk, alg, nonce), signs the CIC and ID token under the GQ signature._x000D_
3. The workload then immediate deletes the OPs RSA signature on the ID Token._x000D_
_x000D_
The CIC is included as part of the GQ protected header of the ID Token. Thus, when the GQ signature signs the new protected header, it also commits to the CIC. As is currently done with GQ signatures, the original protected header of the ID Token is base64 encoded and included in the protected header signed by the GQ signature._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
payload: {_x000D_
  "iss": "gitlab.example.com",_x000D_
  "aud": "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN:1234567890",_x000D_
  ..._x000D_
} _x000D_
signatures: [_x000D_
  {"protected": {"typ": "JWT", "alg": "GQ256", "kid":  Base64(origProtected), _x000D_
  "cic": SHA3_256(upk=alice-pubkey, alg=ES256, rz=crypto.Rand()),_x000D_
  "signature": GQSIGN(RSA-sig, (payload, signatures[0].protected))`_x000D_
  },_x000D_
  {"protected": {"upk": alice-pubkey, "alg": "EC256", "rz": <rz>},_x000D_
  "signature": <SIGN(alice-signkey, (payload, signatures[1].protected))>_x000D_
  },_x000D_
]_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
## Verifying a Gitlab PK Token_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Check the aud claim is prefixed with "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN-" and that the rest of the aud claim matches the expected aud claim._x000D_
2. Check that CIC signature verifies,_x000D_
3. Check that the CIC protected header values are committed to in the cic claim in protected header of GQ signature and that the GQ signature verifies for gitlabs public key._x000D_
_x000D_
## Security_x000D_
_x000D_
If configured correctly, this is approach offers the same security as the approach used with github. However this approach does introduce a  security risk of misconfiguration not present in the github case. If a GQ signature is not used and an attacker learns the ID Token, the attacker can compute the GQ signature from the RSA signature and insert their own public key. _x000D_
_x000D_
We mitigate the risk of this occurring by:_x000D_
_x000D_
* Requiring that PK Tokens that use the GQ signature to attest to the CIC must have "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN-" prefixed in the audience and that they are not considered valid PK Tokens otherwise. This also prevents attacks in which a gitlab ID Token not intended for use as a PK Token is replayed as a PK Token. Note that this rule does not apply to other types of PK Tokens._x000D_
* Ensuring that OpenPubkey clients always enforces the deletion of the RSA signature and only generates GQ signature PK Tokens for gitlab._x000D_
_x000D_
We argue that this sort of misconfiguration is very unlikely because outside of OpenPubkey, ID Tokens are treated as highly sensitive authentication secrets and within OpenPubkey we prevent this misconfiguration. Someone must configure their gitlab to put "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN-" in the aud claim, not use the OpenPubkey protocol and then must expose the ID token to an attacker. We can not prevent people from writing their own insecure protocols._x000D_
_x000D_
## Cosigner (Optional)_x000D_
We propose a security enhancement that adds a cosigner to remove the gitlab OP as a single point of compromise. It also provides additional protection against replay attacks, however we consider this protection to be unnecessary given the other safeguards above._x000D_
_x000D_
The aud claim can be postfixed by a commitment to a public key, `cpk`, whose corresponding signing key, `csk`, configured in gitlabs secret manager. This signing key can be used by the workload to sign the CIC in addition to the GQ signature._x000D_
_x000D_
Since this signing key's public key is committed to in the aud claim in the ID Token, an ID Token even with a aud claim prefixed with "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN-" and the RSA signature is no longer sufficient to attest to the CIC._x000D_
_x000D_
```_x000D_
payload: {_x000D_
  "iss": "gitlab.example.com",_x000D_
  "aud": "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN-CPK"+SHA3_256(cpk),_x000D_
  ..._x000D_
} _x000D_
signatures: [_x000D_
  {"protected": {"typ": "JWT", "alg": "GQ256", "kid":  Base64(origProtected), _x000D_
  "cic": SHA3_256(upk=alice-pubkey, alg=ES256, rz=crypto.Rand()),_x000D_
  "signature": GQSIGN(RSA-sig, (payload, signatures[0].protected))`_x000D_
  },_x000D_
  {"protected": {"upk": alice-pubkey, "alg": "EC256", "rz": <rz>},_x000D_
  "signature": <SIGN(alice-signkey, (payload, signatures[1].protected))>_x000D_
  },_x000D_
  {"protected": {"cospk": cosigner-pubkey, "alg": "EC256"_x000D_
  "cic": SHA3_256(upk=alice-pubkey, alg=ES256, rz=crypto.Rand()),_x000D_
  },_x000D_
  "signature": <SIGN(cosigner-signkey, (payload, signatures[2].protected))>_x000D_
  },_x000D_
]_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Any OpenPubkey verifier configured to expect this audience claim can check this cosigner signature. This removes the gitlab OP as a single point of compromise. This approach can be adapted to JWKS URIs, but changing the aud claim to use be "OPENPUBKEY-PKTOKEN-CPK"+Cosigner-JWKS-URI_x000D_
_x000D_

column26: Singleton to manage user's browser window
column28:
We share the same browser window we open on the user's browser across the OP chooser, the provider and the cosigner. This requires redirecting the browser window as needed for each of these using channels. This is results in hard to reason about code. Instead we should have a singleton that each of these can subscribe to and then use this manage redirects.

- The browser window manager singleton could also manage a single localhost webserver for each of these and track subscriptions such that when there were no more references to it it could always shut down the server.
- If implemented as a interface, we could easily mock this out. Currently the channels significantly increase the complex of unittests.

It could be useful to provide information about the used certificate when verifying a blob or OCI image in JSON for further consumption._x000D_

Let's assume we have a Linux package maintainer. A project X builds source tarballs with Github Actions and signs them. These source tarballs are then released on their website and on Github._x000D_
_x000D_

The Linux package maintainer only checks the website, downloads a tampered source tarball and valid signature, but when checking the issuer and the URI field the Linux maintainer would know that something is wrong._x000D_
_x000D_
_x000D_
This not real cosign output depicts the problem:_x000D_

Project X located at github.com/projectX/projectX creates a new tarball and signature. The related certificate has the following URI and Issuer:_x000D_
```_x000D_
URI: https://github.com/ProjectX/ProjectX/.github/workflows/goreleaser.yml@refs/tags/v0.3.1_x000D_
Issuer:  https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_

column12: cosign doesn't correctly respect individual TSA certificate chains
column26: cosign doesn't correctly respect individual TSA certificate chains
column28:
**Description**

I have a private Sigstore instance, in which I attempted to rotate the TSA certificate chain. When trying to verify any blob/image after the rotation, I get the following error:

```
$ cosign --verbose verify-blob --certificate-identity=kilgore@kilgore.trout --bundle signed.bundle to-sign --rfc3161-timestamp=timestamp.txt --use-signed-timestamps
Error: unable to load TSA certificates: TSA certificate chain must contain exactly one leaf certificate
main.go:74: error during command execution: unable to load TSA certificates: TSA certificate chain must contain exactly one leaf certificate
```

This is because the `GetTSACerts` function in `pkg/cosign/tsa.go` only expects to parse out a single certificate chain, because of the assumption that these individual chains are provided as individual TUF targets.

However in order to be able to properly rotate the TSA certificate chain, one needs to provide the whole TSA certificate chain as a single TUF target (which is possible and I do it). However, when I attempt to introduce a new TSA chain as a new TUF target and keeping the old one as "Expired", I get the above error when verifying any artifact.

I think the `GetTSACerts` function should behave more like `GetRekorPubs`, which returns multiple keys and all of them are considered valid for verification.

I think this will actually work fine in the future with https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/3844 because of how the [timestamp verification function from sigstore-go](https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-go/blob/main/pkg/verify/tsa.go#L87) works. I can submit a PR to fix this if you think it's still worth it before https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/3844 gets merged - I think it's worth because of private Sigstore deployments that might be slower to upgrade.

**Version**

2.4.1, but applies to latest main branch as well AFAICS

column28:
**Description**

In previous changes, support for the OCI Referrers API was added:

* https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/3889 for `attest` and `verify-attestation`.
* https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/2684 for `sign`, `attach`, and `download`.


But, support was never added to `cosign tree`. If I sign, attach, or attest to a container image, those results don't appear in the results of `cosign tree`.

I was thinking that if we put this behind a `cosign tree --experimental-oci11` flag, then it would make sense for cosign tree to display *all artifacts found*, both those located by the convention implemented by `cosign triangulate` and those located by the OCI 1.1 Referrers API.

Something like this:

```
❯ ./cosign tree --experimental-oci11 quay.io/rbean/tree-scsa:example
📦 Supply Chain Security Related artifacts for an image: quay.io/rbean/tree-scsa:example
└── 🔐 Signatures for an image tag: quay.io/rbean/tree-scsa:sha256-b3454025ce78fa93aba879b2824a06a59e2b8c5005b2a4286368433cd0f41cde.sig
   └── 🍒 sha256:ef4e39921eeb670ea453be070877d0fef225a13f97a9f9bf107d4d04d4c0dba6
└── 💾 Attestations for an image tag: quay.io/rbean/tree-scsa:sha256-b3454025ce78fa93aba879b2824a06a59e2b8c5005b2a4286368433cd0f41cde.att
   ├── 🍒 sha256:105da535ba7425024b03685048c33a458b3147315458fc1291479bae34f34997
   └── 🍒 sha256:98c6b2784ffe8a38cc4533d9a5d845cfe4ce72c2aa7e7f00a0682718d0259472
└── 🔗 application/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle.v0.3+json artifacts via OCI referrer: quay.io/rbean/tree-scsa@sha256:01ca3469ae921632f7bd965cb34f9c10f07a723ea68223008871e86052bcfec8
   └── 🍒 sha256:a336d1bfe93e60ae8a5cbbe546663517719d8f3ce1e628ffc0196c0cdf658314
```

(I already prepared a patch for this at https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/pull/4205, but I was stopped by the pull request template which suggested that an issue should be on file with some time to discuss the right approach first.)

[Design doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1QLTMgjX7n74PyNpp3SIxsH7vbak8k-EoylttR25gBXM/edit#heading=h.dgwm7wkem51s)_x000D_
_x000D_
From the work to support embedded SCTs, coupled with a desire to be able to scale beyond 25 QPS, I've written up a doc on the work to reconfigure the production instance of Fulcio as an intermediate CA._x000D_
_x000D_
tl;dr - An in-memory signing key is generated on each server initialization. Fulcio requests an intermediate CA certificate from the managed GCP root, periodically refreshing it. This work involves adding a new CA implementation, which would be a combination of the ephemeral and file CAs._x000D_
_x000D_
This has many benefits:_x000D_
* No outbound calls to create and sign certificates_x000D_
* Ability to scale up QPS significantly_x000D_
* Minimizes the risk of signing key leakage_x000D_
* Automates the process of fetching intermediate CA certs (less operational overhead)

column12: Proposal: Combine the individual OIDC extensions into a single extension
column26: Proposal: Combine the individual OIDC extensions into a single extension
column28:
This is a breakout of the unrelated discussion/proposal in #981, where this was originally brought up incidentally._x000D_
_x000D_
## Problem statement_x000D_
_x000D_
At the moment, Fulcio-issued certificates contain a bunch of X.509 extensions, roughly one per claim in the corresponding OIDC credential/identity. For example, the extension with OID `1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14` is expected to hold a value corresponding to the "Source Repository Ref," which will be the `git` ref for things like GitHub Actions._x000D_
_x000D_
This works perfectly fine, and corresponds roughly to how other PKI ecosystems use X.509 extensions. At the same time, it has a few deficiencies:_x000D_
_x000D_
### Strict compliance_x000D_
_x000D_
X.509 extensions are defined by RFC 5280 as:_x000D_
_x000D_
```asn1_x000D_
   Extension  ::=  SEQUENCE  {_x000D_
        extnID      OBJECT IDENTIFIER,_x000D_
        critical    BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,_x000D_
        extnValue   OCTET STRING_x000D_
                    -- contains the DER encoding of an ASN.1 value_x000D_
                    -- corresponding to the extension type identified_x000D_
                    -- by extnID_x000D_
        }_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Critically, `extnValue` is required to be a nested DER encoding, which most of the OIDC claims are not (instead, they embed the raw value of the claim as bytes)._x000D_
_x000D_
The three solutions here are to:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Define the problem away by defining our own ASN.1 structure (see proposal below), in which OIDC claim values can be raw rather than wrapped in DER;_x000D_
2. Go through a migration period, where existing OIDC claim extensions are duplicated with correctly encoded ones;_x000D_
3. Both of the above._x000D_
  _x000D_
### Space efficiency_x000D_
_x000D_
Encoding each OIDC claim as its own X.509 extension is not space efficient, leading to larger certificate encodings (and thus larger transparency log entries) than strictly necessary. _x000D_
_x000D_
In particular:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Separate extensions means a linear overhead of N `SEQUENCE` payloads;_x000D_
2. Correctly encoded extensions require a linear overhead of N nested DER payloads;_x000D_
3. Each migration away from old claim encodings requires a linear overhead of claim values with new OIDs._x000D_
_x000D_
### Domain separation_x000D_
_x000D_
At the moment, the OIDC claim extensions are the only custom claims added by Fulcio. They can be considered "authenticated," in the sense that they are not only bound to the certificate itself but also derived directly from the original identity token._x000D_
_x000D_
In the future, Fulcio may choose to introduce additional extensions, ones that wouldn't be considered "authenticated" in the same way. Introducing those into the same "namespace" (of extensions) as the OIDC claims could potentially result in user and developer confusion about the provenance and trustworthiness of their extension values._x000D_
_x000D_
See also #1131 for some motivation for this part, although I think the notion of "domain separation" in this context is independently valuable._x000D_
_x000D_
## Proposed solution_x000D_
_x000D_
My proposed solution is to replace N X.509 extensions for N OIDC claims with a single X.509 extension. _x000D_
_x000D_
Two proposed structures for this extension:_x000D_
_x000D_
Proposal 1:_x000D_
_x000D_
```asn1_x000D_
Claims ::= SEQUENCE OF Claim_x000D_
_x000D_
Claim ::= SEQUENCE {_x000D_
  id OBJECT IDENTIFIER,_x000D_
  value ANY DEFINED BY id,_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
Proposal 2:_x000D_
_x000D_
```asn1_x000D_
Claims ::= SEQUENCE OF Claim_x000D_
_x000D_
Identifiers ::= SEQUENCE OF OBJECT IDENTIFIER_x000D_
_x000D_
Claim ::= SEQUENCE {_x000D_
  ids Identifiers,_x000D_
  value OCTET STRING, -- defined by ids_x000D_
}_x000D_
```_x000D_
_x000D_
In both of these proposals, the top-level `Claims` definition would then be wrapped in an ordinary X.509 extension, with a new Sigstore-controlled OID._x000D_
_x000D_
Proposal (2) differs primarily from Proposal (1) in that it offers a few key space and forward-compatibility optimizations:_x000D_
_x000D_
1. Each `Claim` has a list of potential identifiers, meaning that future changes to claim OIDs can be accommodated without duplicating `value` by just adding the new OID to the `ids` sequence. This both saves space (no `value` duplication) and makes forward compatibility simpler (no additional extension to search for; no potential dual-state between the "legacy" value and the "new" value)._x000D_
2. `value` is explicitly an OCTET STRING, meaning that it doesn't obligate any nested DER encoding (and doesn't contract RFC 5280, being a nested value within an extension)._x000D_
_x000D_
## Alternatives considered_x000D_
_x000D_
Doing nothing. IMO the current state of affairs is not a *significant* problem; the primary advantages to this proposal would be conceptual purity, strict compliance with RFC 5280, and lower long-term certificate sizes and diminished OID migration friction._x000D_
_x000D_
## Problems identified_x000D_
_x000D_
None, currently._x000D_
_x000D_
This would require a deprecation/migration period, but this is no different from the deprecation requirements for the current "legacy" OIDs/extensions for GitHub-specific OIDC claims. _x000D_
_x000D_
---_x000D_
_x000D_
CC @znewman01 and @haydentherapper for consideration 🙂

Uniqueness *would* be an application-level expectation for both `Claims` and `Identifiers`.) | haydentherapper: Adding a bit more context to my comment in the other thread - This proposed change is solid technically, and if we were to start from scratch, this would be a good option. I don't think it buys us much to do it now though: * This doesn't save any work for clients, as they'll need to accept both certificate formats for verification. You could say that at some point we drop support for separate extensions, but that breaks verification for all existing signed artifacts out there, and it means we may not see adoption of new client versions that do drop support. * The space savings are O(bytes), I don't expect the addition of a lot more claims. * ASN.1 is complex, and I'd prefer to not maintain structures if we don't have to. * We already fixed the incorrect encoding for the new extensions we added, where each is now a DER string (could be another type too). This leaves 6 duplicated extensions (5 of which were going to be duplicated because they were GitHub specific).

Edward13ruf: My approach involved creating a simple CSR (can be anything) and using [aws-kms-sign-csr](https://github.com/g-a-d/aws-kms-sign-csr/blob/master/aws-kms-sign-csr.py) to sign it. I then passed it to my root CSA and asked it to sign the CSR using the [`SubordinateCACertificate_PathLen0_APIPassthrough/V1`](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/privateca/latest/userguide/UsingTemplates.html#SubordinateCACertificate_PathLen0-V1) template. I gave it an ExtendedKeyUsageType of CODE_SIGNING and filled in all the usual subjects and common names when I passed the CSR through to the CA for signing. I was able to pass this information through using the [--api-passthrough](https://awscli.amazonaws.com/v2/documentation/api/latest/reference/acm-pca/issue-certificate.html) option, hence the need for that particular template. The KMS key in particular was RSA_4096 and I passed it through to Fulcio using `awskms:///<kms_arn>` along with a certificate bundle containing both the root CA public key and the KMS backed intermediate public key I signed above. I did all of this in terraform, but was able to achieve a nice reliable and repeatable pattern once I'd figured out all the steps I needed.

column28:
## Background_x000D_
_x000D_
https://github.com/C2SP/C2SP/blob/main/signed-note.md defines the specification for a signed note, which is the format of a [checkpoint](https://github.com/C2SP/C2SP/blob/main/tlog-checkpoint.md). Note that this specification was only recently created. When checkpoints were added to Rekor, we followed the code for Go's checksum db note format, which is the signed note format - [docs](https://pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/exp/sumdb/internal/note), [code](https://cs.opensource.google/go/x/exp/+/refs/tags/sumdb/v0.0.2:sumdb/internal/note/note.go)_x000D_
_x000D_
The signature is the following format:_x000D_
_x000D_
`— <key name> base64(32-bit key ID || signature)`_x000D_
_x000D_
where key ID is the following format, roughly the truncated hash of the key name, signature scheme, and public key:_x000D_
_x000D_
`key ID = SHA-256(key name || 0x0A || signature type || public key)[:4]`_x000D_
_x000D_
Go's checksum db note code only defines a verifier for ed25519 keys ([code](https://cs.opensource.google/go/x/exp/+/refs/tags/sumdb/v0.0.2:sumdb/internal/note/note.go;l=387)), again aligning with the spec, where signature type = `0x01`. It does not support ecdsa keys._x000D_
_x000D_
For historical reasons (citation needed) and as noted in the spec, ecdsa key IDs are the truncated hash of the DER encoded public key in SPKI format ([code](https://github.com/sigstore/rekor/blob/main/pkg/util/signed_note.go#L52-L61), with the truncation happening [here](https://github.com/sigstore/rekor/blob/main/pkg/util/signed_note.go#L119-L120))._x000D_
_x000D_
## Issue_x000D_
_x000D_
When Rekor generates a signed note, it generates the key ID as a truncated DER encoded public key hash regardless of signature type. ecdsa is spec compliant, but ed25519 and RSA is not. The impact of this is if we were to switch to ed25519 or RSA signing keys, Rekor checkpoints would not be verifiable by omniwitness, armored witness or any other upcoming witness implementations._x000D_
_x000D_
The other issue is that the c2sp spec doesn't define support for RSA. There is an issue tracking this request, but general consensus is a lack of interest in supporting RSA due to additional signature support for witnesses, RSA vulnerability concerns and key/signature size. For public instances that could join a witness network, we should strongly recommend using ecdsa or ed25519 keys. For private instances, RSA can still be supported using the `0xff` identifier type as per the spec._x000D_
_x000D_
## Fixes_x000D_
_x000D_
Given the last time I made a change to the checkpoint format, dropping the timestamp, it impacted clients, I want to make sure we thoughtfully roll this out._x000D_
_x000D_
Clients will need to add support for parsing signed notes following the spec, particularly computing the key ID differently for ed25519 and RSA keys. If you want to avoid any chance of breakage for private deployments that are currently using these key types, you could fallback to the DER encoded public key ID._x000D_
_x000D_
**However**, I don't know if clients were using the key ID to verify checkpoints. If the client was simply dropping the 32-bit key ID from `base64(32-bit key ID || signature)` before verifying the signature, this change seems quite safe to do. For example, for sigstore-go (which uses the Rekor library), we're doing just that - [`Base64`](https://github.com/sigstore/rekor/blob/main/pkg/util/signed_note.go#L175) is the signature without the key ID (`Hash`). Technically this isn't following the spec, as the key ID should be compared against a known key. That doesn't seem like a requirement for Sigstore though, more for witnesses, since we have a way of distributing trusted keys. (Edit: this is not true for other clients, so we will need client changes)_x000D_
_x000D_
For server side changes, given the public instance has only used ecdsa, we could fix the format for ed25519 and RSA signing keys without any impact to clients. If we want to do this in a non-breaking way, we would need to introduce the new checkpoint format in another response field for the `/log` API, though I don't like that approach as much as it'll complicate client logic for fetching a checkpoint and prolong this fix.

haydentherapper: Sorry about that rollout, we had assumed the other content in the signed note was considered optional. The good news with this change is that there would be no changes to metadata produced from the public instance, since it uses ecdsa and there would be no changes there. I am unaware of any other public logs. loosebazooka: Wasn't there also something about using a different style of logid for rekor? I can't seem to remember details, but there was no guarantee it was going to continue to be a hash of the public key like CT.
woodruffw: Summarizing to make sure I understand: 1. For non-ECDSA keys, the key ID is defined as `SHA-256(key name || 0x0A || signature type || public key)[:4]`, where `public key` is `DER(SPKI(raw public key))` 2. For ECDSA keys, the key ID is **not** defined, but Rekor chooses to use `SHA-256(public key)[:4]` 3. `sigstore-python` currently only expects ECDSA-based tlogs, and so does (2) unconditionally Is that correct?
haydentherapper: > Wasn't there also something about using a different style of logid for rekor? I can't seem to remember details, but there was no guarantee it was going to continue to be a hash of the public key like CT. Yea, the CT v2 [RFC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9162.html#section-4.4) defined log IDs as OIDs rather than a hash of a public key. The idea being that you might want to reuse a public key across logs but have each log have its own identity. I don't think we'll move away from the log ID being the hash though as most tools expect this, so instead we'll rotate the key the next time we create a new log. > For non-ECDSA keys, the key ID is defined as SHA-256(key name || 0x0A || signature type || public key)[:4], where public key is DER(SPKI(raw public key)) > For ECDSA keys, the key ID is not defined, but Rekor chooses to use SHA-256(public key)[:4] Unfortunately, reading more, the `public key` encoding is a bit messy. * ed25519 public keys use the [32-byte public key byte array](https://github.com/C2SP/C2SP/blob/main/signed-note.md#ed25519-signatures) for the `public key` part of the key ID, which would be for `0x01` ed25519 checkpoint signatures and `0x04` witness cosignatures (which mandate ed25519). * For `0x02` ECDSA checkpoint signatures and `0x05` RFC6962 checkpoints, it is `SHA256(DER(SPKI(raw public key)))`. (Note that there is an open issue to restrict the new RFC6962 checkpoints to only ecdsa, to not deal with RSA) * For RSA, for `0xff` we are on our own. I would recommend `SHA256(DER(SPKI(raw public key)))` for `public key`, and use `0xff` for the signature type. For ECDSA, it is defined in the [spec](https://github.com/C2SP/C2SP/blob/main/signed-note.md#ed25519-signatures:~:text=Note%20that%20the%20key%20ID%20for%20these%20signatures%20is%20the%20truncated%20SHA%2D256%20hash%20of%20the%20DER%20encoded%20public%20key%20in%20SPKI%20format.). It wasn't Rekor that decided the different format for ecdsa, I believe it was either [RFC 6962](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6962#section-3.2) or some of the original witness work, and the spec didn't want to break existing logs using ecdsa. Rekor's key ID is currently `SHA256(DER(SPKI(raw pubkey)))` - [code](https://github.com/sigstore/rekor/blob/main/pkg/util/signed_note.go#L56-L61) > sigstore-python currently only expects ECDSA-based tlogs, and so does (2) unconditionally If you aren't handling RSA or ed25519, then this is even better, as it wouldn't be a breaking client change.
haydentherapper: I just reread what I wrote, and it's kinda messy. so tldr * ed25519-signed checkpoint key ID: `SHA-256(key name || 0x0A || 0x01 || 32-byte Ed25519 public key)[:4]` * ecdsa-signed checkpoint key ID: `SHA-256(DER(SPKI(raw public key)))[:4]` * RSA checkpoint key ID: `SHA-256(key name || 0x0A || 0xFF || SHA-256(DER(SPKI(raw public key))))[:4]` RSA is up for debate if anyone disagrees, since the spec doesn't define RSA keys. Edit: Also, consider we will add PQ keys at some point, and by the spec, we'll need to reuse `0xff`. If you want to do something else, let's decide now.
woodruffw: Wow, what a mess 😄 So, to round it off: clients that want to handle key IDs correctly will need to: 1. Stop assuming that everything is ECDSA 2. Propagate the key type from its representation in `TrustedRoot.tlogs[].public_key` 3. Use the key type to determine the key ID algorithm to apply Did I get that right? If so, that'll be a slightly involved patch to `sigstore-python`, but not too bad 🙂 > RSA is up for debate if anyone disagrees, since the spec doesn't define RSA keys. Please direct me to another issue if this is the wrong place, but: is there a demonstrated (public or private) desire for RSA-based tlogs? Given that RSA sigs are much larger and that RSA signing is generally slower, I was under the impression that it wasn't commonly used for tlogs (despite RFC 6962 allowing it). With that being said, if RSA support is already decided, I have no objection to that key ID format.
haydentherapper: > Stop assuming that everything is ECDSA Correct, particularly adding support for ed25519. > Propagate the key type from its representation in TrustedRoot.tlogs[].public_key > Use the key type to determine the key ID algorithm to apply Correct. Note that at some point, we'll also want to handle `0x04` co-signed checkpoints, signed with ed25519 as per the spec. So the key ID gives you both the signature algorithm and the structure that you're verifying, a checkpoint vs witnessed checkpoint. But that's forward looking > Please direct me to another issue if this is the wrong place, but: is there a demonstrated (public or private) desire for RSA-based tlogs? Given that RSA sigs are much larger and that RSA signing is generally slower, I was under the impression that it wasn't commonly used for tlogs (despite RFC 6962 allowing it). Actually the opposite, RSA is not preferred. I brought this up in https://github.com/C2SP/C2SP/issues/63, and the consensus was a) concerns about RSA vulns particularly for PKCS#1v1.5, b) key/sig size, c) another alg to support. I did point out RFC 6962 allows for it, but since RFC 6962 doesn't have support for checkpoints and C2SP is focused on improving Certificate Transparency, they're fine going off-spec. So if we want to say no RSA for Rekor, I'm OK with that. Rekor does support it currently so we might get some pushback from private instances, so I'd want to ask around. But if we're already in the state where most clients are just supporting ecdsa, then it's not really a breaking change.
loosebazooka: I vote no rsa support unless it's defined in spec, we'd just be setting ourselves up for future incompatibility
bdehamer: I was just looking through the [implementation](https://github.com/sigstore/sigstore-js/blob/main/packages/verify/src/timestamp/checkpoint.ts#L91-L93) in sigstore-js trying to understand what may need to change. Currently, it grabs the first four bytes of the checkpoint signature and uses that to find the correct key from the TrustedRoot by looking at the first four bytes of the listed key IDs. ![Image](https://github.com/sigstore/rekor/assets/398027/bac21a54-d1e3-4202-a790-cf21ff3d70f9) At no point does it attempt to calculate the key ID. Would this change if Rekor were to use an ed25519 key? Or could we assume that the key ID listed in the TrustedRoot would always reflect the appropriate format?
loosebazooka: Interesting, yeah so are logId and keyHint going to use the same transformation over the key? Is it safe to use logId? Or should it always be calculated?
haydentherapper: @bdehamer, that's a good point. For context, the reason we chose the log ID to be the SHA-256 hash of the DER encoded SPKI public key was to follow RFC 6962. Fulcio's CT log already set the log ID to be that, so we followed the same practice for Rekor. To one of @loosebazooka's questions earlier on, the log ID can be whatever we choose it to be. It probably _shouldn't_ be the key, because otherwise you are forced to rotate the key with every log sharding to maintain unique IDs. But we were trying to follow an existing related spec. For ed25519, we can either: * Change https://github.com/sigstore/protobuf-specs/blob/main/protos/sigstore_common.proto#L136-L139 to say that the log ID's key ID is different for ed25519, equaling `SHA-256(key name || 0x0A || 0x01 || 32-byte Ed25519 public key)`. Return this different log ID in the checkpoint and as part of the Rekor entry response. Also this impacts SET verification since the log ID changes. * Leave the log ID as-is, and change only the checkpoint key ID. This would require clients compute the checkpoint key ID to compare. Impacting the SET verification is what concerns me the most. I believe there are assumptions that the log ID always is `SHA256(DER(SPKI(pubkey)))` in most clients. I'd lean towards the second, making this change only for checkpoints. Tangential, for RSA, I'm planning to continue to follow what we're doing for ECDSA for computing the key ID. I don't want to drop RSA support entirely in case someone is using it and I think this means existing client implementations will continue to work without any changes. I'll just discourage RSA for public logs, and we'll make no guarantees that clients implement RSA support. Lemme know if anyone disagrees.
haydentherapper: Also, there is another option, which is simply to state that publicly witnessed Rekor logs must use ecdsa.
haydentherapper: @loosebazooka and I were chatting today about this, and came up with a good compromise that avoids clients needing to know this computation - let's include the checkpoint key ID (the truncated hash) as an optional field in the trust root [`TransparencyLogInstance`](https://github.com/sigstore/protobuf-specs/blob/main/protos/sigstore_trustroot.proto#L33-L43). Clients can then treat the checkpoint key ID as an arbitrary string rather than a constructed identity. I would vote that we make it optional to avoid making this a breaking change to the trust root. If the checkpoint key ID is not set, then the client should assume checkpoint key ID == log ID (which is the case for ecdsa and RSA). For new ed25519 logs, the checkpoint key ID must be set. What do you think @bdehamer @woodruffw?
woodruffw: I like that idea! That makes things pretty simple on the clients side 🙂
bdehamer: Sounds great, love it!
